question: An 80-year-old man is admitted with a sudden picture of aphasia and right hemiparesis. As background highlights, hypertension, well controlled diet and cognitive impairment in the last year under study by his neurologist. Emergency cranial CT demonstrates a left frontal lobar hematoma without contrast enhancement. What is the most likely cause of the hematoma?

options.opa: Arteriovenous malformation masked by the acute hematoma.
options.opc: Vasculitis isolated from the nervous system.

enhanced_information: The most likely cause of the hematoma in the 80-year-old man with aphasia and right hemiparesis is chronic arterial hypertension, given the presence of a left frontal lobar hematoma without contrast enhancement. This is supported by the chain of chronic arterial hypertension leading to weakening of blood vessel walls and increased risk of hemorrhage. The evidence path showing the structure of the blood vessel wall leading to hemorrhage further supports this conclusion.
analysis: The most likely cause of the left frontal lobar hematoma in this 80-year-old man with sudden aphasia and right hemiparesis is amyloid cerebral angiopathy (congophilic angiopathy). This condition is commonly seen in the elderly and can lead to spontaneous lobar hemorrhages, especially in the setting of cognitive impairment.
